title: Pointers
learningGoals: read and write through a pointer

youtube.title: C++ Pointers Explained: &, * and nullptr | C++ Programming EP 42
youtube.description: In this episode you will declare a pointer, read and write through a pointer and tell p from star p, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Pointers · 0:57 Follow the pointer · 1:37 A pointer and its target · 2:07 Second program · 3:07 Recap · 3:37 Bug of the Day · 4:25 Challenge · 4:45 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "POINTERS" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a crab pointing at a box with a long claw; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a crab pointing at a box with a long claw

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet pointers. A pointer is a variable that holds an address. With it, you can reach another variable from far away.

scenes.onScreen: "Pointers": numbered lines (1. A pointer holds an address; 2. Star in a declaration means pointer; 3. Star in front of a pointer means follow it) and an analogy card: a house key tag: the tag is not the house, but it tells you where to go
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A pointer is a variable that holds an address. You declare it with a star after the type. You give it the address of a variable with the ampersand. A star in front of the pointer means follow the address. You can then read or change the box it points to. Think of a key tag with an address. The tag is not the house, but it tells you where to go.
points: Star in a declaration means pointer
Star in front of a pointer means follow it

analogy.title: Pointers
analogy.body: A house key tag: the tag is not the house, but it tells you where to go

scenes.onScreen: pointer.cpp: a pointer reads and changes fish
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Fish is an int with the value three. [HL 6] P is a pointer to an int. It holds the address of fish. [HL 7] Star p means follow the pointer. It reads the box at that address. It prints three. [HL 8] We can also write through the pointer. [HL 9] Fish is now ten. We changed fish without using its name.

scenes.onScreen: the pointer p holds the address of fish, shown as an arrow
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the two boxes. Fish holds ten. P holds the address of fish. The arrow shows that link. Star p follows the arrow to fish. Writing to star p changes fish.

scenes.onScreen: swapptr.cpp: a swap function that takes two addresses
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] The function takes two pointers. [HL 5] T copies the value that a points to. [HL 6] The value at a becomes the value at b. [HL 7] The value at b becomes the old value of a. [HL 12] The caller passes the addresses of x and y. Now x is two, and y is one. This is the C way to swap. Episode twenty-four showed the C plus plus way.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as swapptr dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints two and one.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A pointer holds an address. Two. The ampersand gives the address of a variable. Three. Star in front of a pointer follows it. Four. Writing through a pointer changes the target. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: The ampersand gives the address of a variable.
Star in front of a pointer follows it.
Writing through a pointer changes the target.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A pointer to the wrong type
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We point an int pointer at a double. The compiler says it cannot convert double star to int star. The pointer type tells the computer how to read the bytes. Use a double pointer for a double.

scenes.onScreen: A pointer walked into a bar. It said, I am just here to point out the drinks.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: A pointer walked into a bar. It said, I am just here to point out the drinks.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: change a variable through a pointer
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make an int called score. Make a pointer to it. Add five to score through the pointer, and print score. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: pointers and arrays. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

pointer.cpp: In function 'int main()':
pointer.cpp:6:14: error: cannot convert 'double*' to 'int*' in initialization
    6 |     int* p = &price;
      |              ^~~~~~
      |              |
      |              double*
bug.why: The type of a pointer says how to read the bytes at the address. A pointer to int cannot point at a double.

pun: "A pointer walked into a bar. It said, I am just here to point out the drinks."
challenge: Make an int called score. Make a pointer to it. Add five to score through the pointer, and print score.
challengeAnswer: Write star p plus equals five. Then print score. It shows the new value.
